events.title: Latvian citizen, Russian businessman, German sabotage suspect: who is Oleg Levushkin?

articles.text: Latvian citizen, Russian businessman, German sabotage suspect: who is Oleg Levushkin? Share Follow: Follow LSM on Google 7:02 October 19, 10:30 Crime Authors: Ella Semjonova (LTV "De facto" pētnieciskā žurnāliste) In August, a sabotage attempt took place at Leipzig Airport in Germany, which the German government has said was carried out by Russia. One of the suspected organizers of the attack is a Latvian citizen by the name of Oļegs Ļevuškins (Oleg Levushkin). The Latvian Television investigative programme De Facto revealed on October 18th that Levushkin had been in business in Russia for almost 18 years as the owner of a Latvian pharmaceutical company called "Elpis". The State Security Service (VDD) confirmed to De Facto that it has already initiated the procedure to revoke Levushkin's Latvian citizenship. Leipzig Airport is one of the main routes for delivering military aid to Ukraine. On the evening of August 4 this year, a drone crashed into the wing of a Ukrainian cargo plane there, very close to its fuel tank. The drone contained explosives, but the detonator did not go off. It was only several hours later that an airport employee noticed the crashed drone. The airport suspended flights. That same night, a second drone allegedly crashed into a DHL cargo plane, which was damaged. A third was found near the airport, also carrying traces of what could be explosives. In September, the German government said Russia was behind the sabotage attempts. Foreign investigative journalists have named Latvian citizen Oleg Levushkin as one of the possible organizers of the sabotage, whose contacts with the Russian military intelligence service GRU, according to them, began many years ago. GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov, who is linked to sabotage in Europe, allegedly helped him resolve a business dispute as early as 2007. The Insider has alleged that shortly before the attack, on July 13, Levushkin received a call from an arms dealer named Andrei Usachov, who was in the colonel's circle of contacts. Two weeks later, the Latvian citizen arrived in Germany, where his rented car was spotted at Leipzig Airport. "Levushkin was the one who led and coordinated several Belarusians who were operating drones at the airport. I don't think Levushkin himself piloted any of the drones. I don't think he had the skills to do that. I think he organized the work of this group," Roman Dobrokhodov, editor-in-chief of The Insider , said in an interview with De Facto . Two years ago, The Insider journalists helped Polish authorities identify the same two men who are now part of Levushkin's group. Back then, they were involved in arson at a store in Lodz. Although both were already known to Polish authorities, they were still free to travel around Europe. Now, biological traces of one man have been found on the antenna of a Leipzig drone, while the other's possible involvement is indicated by his movement data. Again, they were not arrested. After the attack, Levushkin bought a plane ticket to Moscow and probably fled to Russia. The VDD confirmed to De Facto that Latvian citizen Levushkin is included in the German investigation. The service is providing German colleagues with information about his previous activities in Latvia, but is not commenting on the investigation in more detail. On social media, 54-year-old Latvian citizen Levushkin presents himself as an avid motorcyclist. He has posted photos from trips around Russia and participated in international motorcycle races, including on a motorcycle registered in Latvia. At one time, Levushkin lived in the Zolitude neighborhood of Rīga. In 2004, Levushkin became the sole owner and manager of the Rīga-registered company "Jana SD" for a few months. This company was engaged in retail trade in markets, but was liquidated in 2017. He left Latvia several years ago, but the apartment in which he had lived was sold only in 2023. Levushkin has been doing business in Russia for a long time. In 2000, the wholesaler of medicines, spices and other goods "IVA" began operating in Pskov - initially as a representative office of the Latvian pharmaceutical company "Elpis". A few years after its founding, Levushkin and another Latvian businessman, Jānis Leitāns, became co-owners of the Russian company "IVA". Their business cooperation lasted almost 18 years. From 2010, Levushkin also managed the company until he left it in 2021. The Pskov company is still operating. Leitāns is still its co-owner – he owns 65% of the company's shares. IVA's turnover in 2025 reached approximately 15 million euros, converted from rubles. Leitāns also controls the Latvian company "Elpis", whose turnover last year reached 47 million euros. The company continues to trade with Russia - according to the annual report, its revenue in this market in 2025 exceeded eight million euros. Leitāns confirmed in a written response to De Facto that Elpis's cooperation with the Pskov company IVA continues even after Levushkin's departure. Spices, dried vegetables, medicinal herbs and medicines are being delivered to Russia. Leitāns emphasizes that deliveries are taking place in compliance with applicable requirements and sanctions. Leitāns claimed that he had not contacted Levushkin for more than six years. "The board of SIA Elpis first learned about the information about Oleg Levushkin's possible involvement in organizing sabotage in Leipzig and his possible ties to the special services of the Russian Federation from the media," Leitāns stated. Levushkin still owns several companies in Russia, mainly in the trade and real estate sectors. One of them was re-registered in occupied Sevastopol in 2025. Levushkin has a Latvian passport - an advantage that Russian special services use in their operations. "This is extremely beneficial for Russian intelligence services, because Russian citizens are checked very carefully when crossing the border. Now it is extremely difficult to use them in any operations," explained Roman Dobrokhodov. In turn, people with Latvian passports, such as Levushkin, are more difficult for European security services to control. As Dobrokhodov explained, they can move freely between countries and are not subject to such strict checks as Russian citizens. "Russia has used this method for a long time with its citizens, who are also trying to obtain citizenships of other countries so that they can operate more freely in different parts of the world," explained Minister of the Interior Jānis Dombrava (National Alliance). Levushkin has both Latvian and Russian citizenship even though Latvian law does not allow such dual citizenship. The VDD confirmed to De Facto that it has already started the procedure to revoke Levushkin's Latvian citizenship. He is not alone. In 2025, the VDD recommended revoking Latvian citizenship for 26 people – 19 citizens and seven 'non-citizens' – for unauthorized dual citizenship or support for an aggressor state. events.title: Russian hackers teamed up to wipe data at Ukrainian grain firm

articles.text: Image: Johannes Plenio / Unsplash Russian hackers teamed up to wipe data at Ukrainian grain firm The Russian state-linked hacking group Sandworm collaborated with another threat actor to carry out a destructive cyberattack against a Ukrainian grain logistics company last year, researchers said Thursday. The attack began in July 2025, when a Russian-aligned espionage group known as UAC-0099 gained access to the unnamed company's systems through a phishing email containing a malicious attachment, according to a report by Slovak cybersecurity firm ESET. The hackers first installed a backdoor called MatchWok to maintain access to the company's network. They later deployed a previously unknown tool, dubbed MythicRatatoskr, that allowed them to run commands remotely, steal files and take screenshots. "We have not seen MythicRatatoskr backdoor used anywhere else, and we found indications that a Linux variant may also exist," said ESET researcher Anton Cherepanov, who investigated the attack. Researchers believe UAC-0099 subsequently handed over access to Sandworm, a group linked by Western intelligence agencies to Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU. Sandworm carried out a data-wiping attack against the company two months later, in September. ESET said it could not determine which of the two groups primarily operated the newly discovered backdoor. The researchers also identified an unusual technique used by the attackers to conceal their communications with infected computers. Instead of connecting directly to a conventional server controlled by the hackers, the malware communicated through Yggdrasil, a decentralized network that allows devices to exchange encrypted data without relying on a central hub. "To our knowledge, this is the first documented case of Yggdrasil being abused in this way by a state-aligned threat actor," the researchers said, warning that such networks could make malicious infrastructure more resilient and harder to trace. UAC-0099, which has been active since at least 2022, has previously targeted Ukrainian government agencies, financial institutions, media outlets and companies in the transportation, manufacturing and energy sectors. Sandworm is among Russia's most notorious state-backed hacking groups, known for targeting critical infrastructure and carrying out destructive operations against Ukraine. The group was linked to cyberattacks that caused power outages in Ukraine in 2015 and 2016, as well as an attempted attack on the country's energy infrastructure in 2022. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Sandworm has repeatedly used data-wiping malware against Ukrainian organizations. Unlike ransomware, which typically encrypts files to demand payment, such malware is designed to permanently destroy data and disrupt operations. In a report published last November, ESET said Sandworm had launched multiple destructive attacks against Ukrainian organizations in the grain, energy, logistics and government sectors between June and September 2025. Although Ukrainian infrastructure has faced frequent cyberattacks throughout the war, direct attacks on agricultural businesses had been relatively uncommon, researchers said. ESET’s findings are another example of cooperation between Russian hacking groups. Earlier in 2025, the firm identified four cases in which two Russia-linked espionage groups, Gamaredon and Turla, both associated with Russia's Federal Security Service, targeted the same Ukrainian organizations. “A UAC-0099-to-Sandworm handoff is unusual in the specific actors involved, but no longer surprising as a pattern,” researchers said. News Nation-state No previous article No new articles Daryna Antoniuk is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.
